what: The score is the fixed-position insertion increase minus the customer's depot–customer–depot standalone cost. Equivalently, it is the negative of the routing saving obtained by merging that customer into the current route rather than serving it alone. It uses only three insertion-edge distances and one depot distance, so each call is O(1) in time and space.
why: Plain cheapest insertion can favor customers near the depot because they have small absolute detours, even when leaving a distant, geographically compatible customer for another route is expensive. The standalone-cost credit counteracts that bias: distant customers score well only when the current route can absorb them with a comparatively small detour. Since routes are seeded by the farthest remaining customer, this tends to grow coherent outward clusters, while the insertion term still penalizes crossing to an incompatible region. It is a parallel Clarke–Wright-style construction criterion and remains meaningful when subsequent 2-opt changes visit order. Its limitations are that the standalone route is only a local comparison, not a prediction of how deferred customers will actually be grouped; it does not explicitly optimize capacity packing or account for demand scarcity, and its usefulness should be validated on both held-out P instances and other CVRP families.
